lesson.title: Three Domains of Life: Redrawing the Tree at Its Deepest Roots
lesson.summary: The three domain system, Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya, classifies life at its broadest level based on molecular comparisons of ribosomal RNA, revealing that Archaea are as distinct from Bacteria as either is from Eukarya.
lesson.body:
The three domain system divides all life into Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya, the broadest and most inclusive level of biological classification, sitting above kingdom. This scheme was proposed by Carl Woese, working with George Fox, in 1977, based on comparing ribosomal RNA gene sequences across a wide range of organisms, an application of the same molecular, phylogenetic comparison methods you have already encountered in other contexts.

Before this work, biologists commonly grouped all prokaryotes, organisms lacking a nucleus, into a single broad category. Woese's ribosomal RNA comparisons overturned that assumption. The sequence data showed that Archaea are genetically as distinct from Bacteria as either group is from Eukarya, even though Archaea and Bacteria share the same basic prokaryotic cell structure you studied earlier, with no nucleus and no membrane bound organelles. Despite that shared structural simplicity, Archaea have distinctive cell membrane lipid chemistry, and some components of their gene expression machinery, including their RNA polymerase, more closely resemble those found in Eukarya than those found in Bacteria. This mix of prokaryotic structure with some distinctly eukaryote-like molecular machinery is part of why Archaea earned their own domain rather than being lumped in with Bacteria.

Briefly, the three domains break down as follows. Bacteria is a highly diverse domain that includes most of the familiar prokaryotes involved in decomposition, disease, and countless other ecological roles. Archaea is also prokaryotic in structure and includes many species found in extreme environments such as hot springs, highly salty water, and oxygen free sediments, though archaea are not limited to extreme habitats and are also common in ordinary environments, including soil and the open ocean. Eukarya includes every organism built from eukaryotic cells: protists, fungi, plants, and animals, a domain whose origin, as covered previously, appears to trace back to an archaeal host cell that took on a bacterial endosymbiotic partner.

The three domain tree is essentially an extremely deep cladogram, built from molecular sequence comparison rather than visible anatomy, since there is no shared physical trait you could observe by eye that would let you correctly group, say, a mushroom with an amoeba rather than with a bacterium. This is phylogenetics operating at the largest possible scale, reconstructing relationships among lineages that diverged so long ago that molecular evidence is essentially the only tool available.

It is worth noting that this classification is not necessarily the final word. More recent studies comparing many genes at once, rather than ribosomal RNA alone, have suggested to some researchers that eukaryotes may have arisen from within the archaeal branch rather than standing as a fully separate, equally ranked domain, a possibility consistent with the Asgard archaea evidence discussed in the context of the origin of eukaryotes. If that view holds up, it would point toward a two domain tree of life with eukaryotes nested inside Archaea, rather than three separate co-equal branches. This remains a genuinely active scientific debate rather than a settled matter, and it is a good example of how classification schemes can be revised as new molecular evidence accumulates.
